learningObjective: Recognize that a shared additive shift leaves softmax probabilities and cross-entropy unchanged but changes log Z, so z-loss selects an anchored representative of the same predictive distribution.
mediumRationale: A three-column semantic table is the smallest medium that aligns two equivalent logit vectors row by row with their identical probabilities and cross-entropy but different log partitions and penalties. The exact arithmetic makes the otherwise invisible degree of freedom concrete.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected: this is an arithmetic invariance rather than a process graph, and automatic routing would not align equal and unequal quantities precisely.
mediumComparison.svg: Rejected: no continuous geometry is needed, while fixed SVG text would make the worked values harder to select and reflow.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Selected: table headers expose the comparison relationships, values remain selectable, and the established table primitive fits the reading column and print.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: an offset slider could generate more examples but would hide the invariant behind controls; one exact nonzero shift proves it statically.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: the source figures show training dynamics and numerical formats rather than this invariance. No permission assumption or external artwork is needed for an original calculation.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: prose states cancellation algebraically, but readers must still hold five linked quantities in working memory to see what changes and what cannot change.

pages.insight: The section divider opens the classification-loss sequence inspected for cross-entropy and softmax context.
The classification slide relates negative log-likelihood to cross-entropy, gives the softmax normalization equation, and recommends fused log-softmax for numerical stability.
The neighboring slide discusses convex and non-convex losses but adds no logit-shift or log-partition treatment.

The next classification slide explicitly demonstrates that subtracting one constant from every logit leaves softmax unchanged and prevents exponential overflow, the closest deck analogue to the shared-shift mental model.
The following slide moves to surrogate losses, ending the local softmax sequence without introducing z-loss.
The preceding LLM-data slide establishes the large-language-model context but contains no loss or precision mechanism.
The LLM-training slide says softmax is run in full precision for stability while most operations use bfloat16, supplying relevant mixed-precision context without a logit penalty.
The neighboring compute-optimization slide introduces attention softmax and BF16/FP16 numerics, then moves from output-loss stability to attention systems.
The sequence-packing slide concerns masking and throughput and provides no additional z-loss evidence.
The FlashAttention slide tracks a running maximum and softmax denominator for stable normalization, reinforcing log-sum-exp numerics in a different softmax application.
The speculative-decoding slide precedes the deck's dedicated mixed-precision treatment and contains no z-loss analogue.
The mixed-precision slide compares FP16, BF16, and FP32 and again recommends FP32 for LayerNorm, softmax, and loss, but does not constrain upstream logit magnitude.
The following training-and-serving summary closes the precision neighborhood without mentioning z-loss.

deckReview.notes: All 214 physical pages of the local PDF were text-indexed for z-loss, log partition, partition function, softmax, logit, numerical stability, BF16, and FP8. Every match was reviewed. The complete neighborhoods on pages 32-36, 106-115, and other isolated softmax references were examined. Page 35 is the closest conceptual source because it shows shared-shift invariance; pages 107 and 114 provide precision context. The deck contains no z-loss definition, final-logit penalty, or reusable figure.
deckReview.license: No general reuse license was identified in the local deck, and it includes externally sourced material. It is treated as review-only; no screenshot, artwork, wording, values, or layout is reproduced.

sources.title: ST-MoE: Designing Stable and Transferable Sparse Expert Models
sources.usage: Used as the primary derivation and stability source for squared log-partition z-loss, its gradient pressure on exponentiated logits, and its role in reducing low-precision roundoff. The paper applies it to router logits and identifies it as an adaptation of final-softmax z-loss.

sourceReview.notes: The calculation starts from p = (0.70, 0.20, 0.10) and logits log p, for which Z = 1 and log Z = 0. Adding c = 5 to every logit multiplies every unnormalized exponential by e^5, so normalization cancels it and both p and target-A cross-entropy remain 0.357 nats. Log Z increases by exactly 5; with lambda_z = 10^-4 the added penalty is 10^-4 times 25 = 0.0025. This isolates the common-offset degree of freedom. It does not claim z-loss directly limits relative gaps, reproduces a paper experiment, or proves universal training gains.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected the exact loss and mixed-precision neighborhoods, then verified the definition and coefficient in ST-MoE and PaLM and the cooldown evidence in Marin before selecting an original exact-arithmetic comparison.

implementation.accessibility: The figure has a linked learning question, a real table with scoped row and column headers, and a complete aria-label that states every value and inference. Explicit equal values and written labels carry the comparison without color. The established fixed-layout table uses wrapping text with no minimum width at 390 CSS pixels, theme tokens preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print rules force a light, high-contrast, page-break-safe rendering.
